segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: OK, William, we are gonna talk for little bit. I'm gonna ask you some questions, I'm just gonna follow what they have on this paper.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: This recording they are doing, they are gonna record us talkin'. The fluent Cherokee speakers are passing, it might be just us that don't know how to speak Cherokee. [laughs]

segments.speaker: william-chewey
segments.translation: It's just gonna be Cherokee with us [laughs] and if we try to speak English, we won't be able to… [laughs]

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: And these that are learning the language, they are teaching, they might learn something. They are fighting for the Cherokee language, like what we are doing. Or them teaching, because really the Cherokee language is dying.

segments.speaker: william-chewey
segments.translation: Are the kids gonna use this recording that we are doing?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah…

segments.speaker: william-chewey
segments.translation: That's good if the ones speaking the language hear it.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, that's true.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: So, the first question is, what is your name in English and in Cherokee?

segments.speaker: william-chewey
segments.translation: My name is William Chewey in English and in Cherokee is Wah-woshe.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: What does that mean or who?

segments.speaker: william-chewey
segments.translation: Well, someone in our family that was in the military, that was his name. That's what my mother told me, but I don't know who it is. She told me someone's name was Wah-woshe. I don't know how true it is, but some old man told me that my voice sounds like something dripping, like when it rains, the dripping he said. [laughs] Or I told them I fell off a roof when I was born. [laughs]

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Where were you born?

segments.speaker: william-chewey
segments.translation: I was born in Piney. There were no hospitals back then when we were kids. Right by Piney church, there is a driveway by a big hill – there's an old house.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Is that house still there?

segments.speaker: william-chewey
segments.translation: Yeah, that house is still there.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: It's not where Salode used to live, is it?

segments.speaker: william-chewey
segments.translation: No, no that's not it. There was someone that lived there last, but I forgot who it is. I can't remember. Before they built that new house across the road – the house is not fairly new. A long time ago the house was really old – and right there below the hill they used to get water down there.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, there used to be spring water coming out of there. Sale used to live there and down that hill was where the spring water used to be. When it was wintertime they used to put us to work goin' and getting water. [laughs] I don't know why, but we always used to like going to Sale's house, because they would put us to work all the time. [laughs]

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: About what year was it?

segments.speaker: william-chewey
segments.translation: Uhhhh… 'bout ‘53, but I forget. Prolly ‘bout 1953.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: So where did you grow up at?

segments.speaker: william-chewey
segments.translation: Right where we live now, around Sycamore. That area, that's where my father worked at, but I was just a little boy back then. And then we moved towards Piney in the holler. We lived there for a little bit, I think it was Scott Phillip’s property.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Was it at Stick Springs?

segments.speaker: william-chewey
segments.translation: Yeah, that's it, right past there. And then Salode used to live right there on top of the hill.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, I remember that place.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Has it changed a lot from when you grew up at, from now and then?

segments.speaker: william-chewey
segments.translation: Yeah, kinda seems like it. Yeah, a lot of people – well mostly a lot of people – have changed nowadays. Or they might have been like that, and I'm just now finding out. I don't know, that's what seems like nowadays. I didn't think that it would be like this. I'm 70 years now, and when I was a teenager…

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Like we talked about where you grew up at, that's pretty much where you been all your life.

segments.speaker: william-chewey
segments.translation: And where we live now, when we moved in Piney that's when I started going to school.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Whenever you lived in Six Springs, do you remember how it was like around there? There used to be a creek there…

segments.speaker: william-chewey
segments.translation: Yeah there used to be a creek just right there, and nowadays the creek is way over there and it's just a little creek now. A long time ago it used to be big creek and had big fish in there all the time, we would go get our gigs if nobody seen us I'd be chasing them fish around, or we would be swimming in there.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: How 'bout back then, there used to be people living by there.

segments.speaker: william-chewey
segments.translation: Yeah, there used to be little houses there. Dale and Dawn used to live there. There used to be 'bout three houses, little ones right by the turn off, by Six Springs. They used to live right there.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: That person, we was talkin' earlier – Mose. His mom and dad, they call him Run About.

segments.speaker: william-chewey
segments.translation: Think his name John Litta, that's who lived there.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: And then Sequoia.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: What comes to your mind when you think about where you grew up at?

segments.speaker: william-chewey
segments.translation: I guess what it was like and people that has passed on who I remember. Really there has been a lot of them that has passed on that are the same age as me that I grew up with. Everything has changed and if we went to the creek somewhere there was nothing to be scared of back then. There was nothing to be afraid of, because where we live now right by Beaty Creek, where the Dority houses are, we used to walk all the way over there 'bout two or three of us boys. We would walk through the woods, and we would stay there all day. There was nothing dangerous about it just sometimes there would be someone show up that was drunk, but we all laughed around and there was nothing dangerous about it. [laughs]

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: [laughs] It wasn't the people that live there close coming out. [laughs]

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: You're still working, right?

segments.speaker: william-chewey
segments.translation: Yeah, I'm still working for the people from Tulsa. He an attorney, but the old man that hired me the first time passed away. But that boy took over everything. We don't farm, but they raise cows. I watch them and then nowadays I bale hay. That young boy, he's not that tight, but that old man he's very tight. [laughs] Nowadays, I have tractors and they all have air conditioning, so I'm doing good now. [laughs] Even if I'm not doing anything, I'm always in one of them where it's cool. [laughs]

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Do you have any hobbies?

segments.speaker: william-chewey
segments.translation: No, not really. A long time ago I used to play marbles. Last time I went and played, I was missing everything. I guess they got mad at me. [laughs] They didn't even tell me to come back. [laughs] But nowadays I don't do much. I just sit around and try not to do much.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: So, you're just sitting around resting?

segments.speaker: william-chewey
segments.translation: I'll be sitting around in shade somewhere. A long time ago I grew up in town. But now where I live all you hear is birds and sometimes you will get chickens. That's what I like most these days.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: Where you live now, is it still your family or just other people living around there?

segments.speaker: william-chewey
segments.translation: No, not really. Pretty much all the ones that live there are the people from overseas. Them kind of people have houses there, but one is a [unclear], that lives there. But there was an old lady living, but she passed away a while back. But there are people from Jay living there. That boy is OK. They all live around that area. They pretty much bought all that land, but my aunt lives towards Sycamore, where Abby and Tommy live or is from. But even though they live pretty close, it’s hard to go visit one another. I don't know if we are just living life too fast or what but it's hard to see one another.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Nowadays, the days are going by pretty fast. Seems like we just don't have time to visit one another, because used to. We would go visit one another. It's not like that now. Days are going by too fast.

segments.speaker: william-chewey
segments.translation: If I'm doing something and I stop and think, “I'm gonna go see this person,” that's the only time I go visit someone. But if I just think about it and say, “Well, I'll just go visit them tomorrow,” I will never make it.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, that's what really happens.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: How many were y'all in the family?

segments.speaker: william-chewey
segments.translation: There was four of us. Franklin and Jawana are deceased. It's just me and John now.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: What was your dad's sister's name that used to live with y'all?

segments.speaker: william-chewey
segments.translation: Ga-wehg.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Is she still alive?

segments.speaker: william-chewey
segments.translation: Yeah, she still alive. She lives in Alaska.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: She left for good, huh?

segments.speaker: william-chewey
segments.translation: Yeah, she left for good, yeah, and that's what happens. Last time she came down, she said she didn't speak Cherokee. She said she forgot everything she knew, because, really she didn't speak Cherokee the whole time she was up there. Yeah, she came down for a little bit when our father passed away. Well, she also came down when we had our family reunion.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Boy, she used to speak really good Cherokee.

segments.speaker: william-chewey
segments.translation: Oh yeah, she did, well and we was around our mom and dad – that's all we used to speak.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: So y'all used to get in trouble in Cherokee? [laughs] I bet John did for sure. [laughs]

segments.speaker: william-chewey
segments.translation: I guess John really didn't understand Cherokee. That's why he got in trouble all the time. [laughs] Or probably both of us. [laughs]

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: [laughs] John didn't understand anything. [laughs]

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: How 'bout you? Do you still talk to someone in Cherokee in your family all the time?

segments.speaker: william-chewey
segments.translation: Yeah, John. Just me and him in our family. But now he lives in Proctor or around Christy.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: He lives all the way over there now?

segments.speaker: william-chewey
segments.translation: I told him, “Everyone around knew who you were. You thought you was hiding over there.” [laughs] Yeah, if I talk to him on the telephone all we speak is Cherokee, because nowadays, even if it's someone that speaks real good Cherokee, it's hard for them to talk Cherokee some of them. I don't know why, but it's like that. If I know someone that speaks Cherokee, I'll talk to them in Cherokee, because they will understand it if they know Cherokee. If I see Rob Daurity, I speak to him in Cherokee. You don't know him do you? [laughs] You wouldn't want to know him. Me and him grew up together also.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: How many kids do you have?

segments.speaker: william-chewey
segments.translation: I have two girls, and I have three grandkids, two girls and one boy.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: How old are they?

segments.speaker: william-chewey
segments.translation: Well, that boy is five years old and one of the girls is eight, and the other one will be 10 soon. Her birthday is Saturday. That little boy and his grandma are around here somewhere. That's who dropped me off.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Oh, OK.

segments.speaker: william-chewey
segments.translation: [laughs] If they see a Walmart, they always think they have to go there. [laughs]

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: [laughs] So that's where they are spending all the money? [laughs]

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: What were your parents' names and then your grandparents’?

segments.speaker: william-chewey
segments.translation: My dad's name was (Ge-nuge) and my mom's name was (Wei-ghe) was her name.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: How 'bout their parents? What were their names?

segments.speaker: william-chewey
segments.translation: Their mom's name was (Salode) and their dad’s was (Ja-ude).

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Where did they live where they grew up?

segments.speaker: william-chewey
segments.translation: It was around Honey Creek – I think somewhere around there. I think because they said when they built that lake around here, they lost some land, they said. They were from around that area somewhere.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, that's what happened to us – Oluchi, they bought all the land that's when we had to move out of there.

segments.speaker: william-chewey
segments.translation: Over at my father's place, there was place called… Oi-gonce, he live in Zu-wi and my father’s mother their last child... Think his last name was Stal. I don't know the first name. They were already passed on, but Oi-gonce used to live with us sometimes.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Oh, yeah. So he used to come around sometimes. Salode used to live around there pretty close?

segments.speaker: william-chewey
segments.translation: Yeah, over by the field across the road is where they used to live, for very long time.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Your mom and dad, did they ever say they met?

segments.speaker: william-chewey
segments.translation: Uh-uh, no they didn't, and I don't know really where they met, and I don't know really. When me dad started coming around, because my dad grew up around Ja-ude around that area.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: If your parents and grandparents were still alive, what would be the most important thing you would ask them?

segments.speaker: william-chewey
segments.translation: I guess where they grew up at, and where they were born and talk to them 'bout the old Cherokee. Did someone teach you where you came from? I guess that would be what I would ask them.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: So, they never really told you anything about where they grew up, that?

segments.speaker: william-chewey
segments.translation: No, not really. Whatever happen while they were growing up, I've never heard anything 'bout them talkin' 'bout it.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, really... What we were talkin' about earlier? If people knew the old Cherokee, well that's where it all started, isn't it? All of our Cherokee names.

segments.speaker: william-chewey
segments.translation: There has been couple people tell me about the name Chewey – means water dog, they were sayin', but I really don't know what it is really.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: What is a water dog?

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: The little... I know it's a watercress.

segments.speaker: william-chewey
segments.translation: Yeah, that's it, but I really don't know. And also, to me Sta-oya, that was Chewey’s name, I think. Or oh-gone-ah-stoze. Me and John were talkin' about it one time. I used to go back to old Cherokee. That was the first thing I checked what water dog was, or salamander, he said.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: What was the name for a water dog?

segments.speaker: william-chewey
segments.translation: I don't know what they call them. And Chewey, I don't know how they put them together, and also the salamander and waterdog. Me, I would rather see Ah-sto standing there. [laughs]

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: You haven't lived anywhere else besides here? Or did you just grow up around here?

segments.speaker: william-chewey
segments.translation: No, just around here. When I was in the eighth grade, I started going to school in Sequoyah. That's where I graduated at and when I graduated, I started working construction everywhere. I don't know when it was when my father got sick with cancer. John and them were all married. They really didn't have time to help take care of him. I told them I would quit working and move back in with him to help him out. I thought it was gonna be temporary, but it’s been 40 years and I'm still there. [laughs]

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: So, you were stuck there and couldn't leave? [laughs]

segments.speaker: william-chewey
segments.translation: But then, when I think about it, if I hadn’t done that, I wouldn't have had kids. I wouldn't have got married, I was making real good money back then, when this man Underwood hired me, but my father wasn't able to feed the cows or do other things. So I told him I would help him just for little bit. I guess I forgot how to eat crawdads, and squirrels, but then I thought, “This is where I belong, this is where I grew up”. When I was goin' to all the other places, that wasn't good. I was doing my own thing. I'm surprised that I'm still here at 70 years old – that's what I was sayin' earlier.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: That's good, because they say it's hard to leave or move out of your home if you been there all your life.

segments.speaker: william-chewey
segments.translation: Yeah, that's what I was sayin'. I was doing OK, if that wasn't the case, I wouldn't have got married, and we wouldn't have kids.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: Well, that's what was meant to happen.

segments.speaker: william-chewey
segments.translation: Someone was either sick or passed away before we came back around. That’s what I think about sometimes. I don't ever tell anyone it's just in my own mind.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: You probably were walkin' in your parents' footsteps.

segments.speaker: william-chewey
segments.translation: Yeah, I live in my own house, and I can just walk outside, and my work is just right there and I'm still late sometimes. [laughs]

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Like you said, sometimes a reunion. I know that your father was always ready to help someone on. Whatever he could, like everyone. Do you still see things like that when people say Ga-dugi?

segments.speaker: william-chewey
segments.translation: No, it's not the same like it used to be nowadays, because my father, you didn't have to ask him. If someone needed help somewhere he was already ready to do whatever. I've lost how to do things a little bit, but sometimes I do something people tell me that's what I need to do, that's what people did growing up and that's what they are asking you to do, if you would just understand. [laughs]

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah and when someone passed away, your dad always helped dig the grave. He was the one always there, and he would ask them, “Where do you want the grave at?” And they would tell him, and he would always go there, wherever they told him.

segments.speaker: william-chewey
segments.translation: Yeah, back then they dug with their bare hands. Sometimes I would go there with him, and they were using the kerosene lantern for light. They would dig all night at the cemetery.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: So in the morning time, it will be ready. That's what they used to do. That I remember, and when we say everyone, everyone did that. It wasn't like they were gonna just say they are gonna do it.

segments.speaker: william-chewey
segments.translation: He also worked in the church committee, whatever they needed to do to make money, even selling pies, or selling ice cream. Or when they meet quarterly, they would cook hog meat. There would be a lot of people show up.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: I remember, if it's in the summertime they sell ice cream. Sometimes I'd see your dad standing over there. [laughs]

segments.speaker: william-chewey
segments.translation: You know that big ice they break up. They put it in a tow sack and break it up, that's what they say they use.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: There used to be a lot of people show up.

segments.speaker: william-chewey
segments.translation: Yeah, a lot of people.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, everyone used to have a good time. Yeah, I used to remember. Like I was sayin', Salode, when she used to live by Piney Church I used to go there for little bit in the summertime. We would be riding bikes. I would ride from Jay. I'd ride all the way there. [laughs] I'd go through Stick Springs.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Do you garden nowadays, if you have time?

segments.speaker: william-chewey
segments.translation: Yeah, I used to, but now... I'm gonna try again this spring. I got a little garden. I planted beans, peas – they are easy to grow. I have a lot of chickens and they always tear my garden up, but I love my chickens so much. I never do anything to them. [laughs] So now we don't buy a lot of things, but, like I said, I'm gonna try again this spring. If it turns out good, then that be nice. There for while we didn't, because we used to have a big garden when we were kids, but my mom, if the garden was going good, then my mother would put a big hat on. Then we knew it was time to go to work. [laughs] And then us kids would run off. [laughs] If you have a good garden, you gotta work hard, but there ain't nothing better than growing your food.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Do you go hunting sometimes?

segments.speaker: william-chewey
segments.translation: Yeah, I still go hunting for squirrels but only sometimes when it's in season. But just around the house because there are a lot of them around the house. But then I started letting people that I know, let them hunt over there. But I told them, “If y'all kill any deer, I want some meat.” So that's what I got used to and I don't hardly hunt anymore. [laughs] So they give me some meat. Well, they clean them at my house, anyway, if they kill anything. I still have some guns, but I'm just not able to go hunt anymore.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: So, you found an easier way to get some eat, huh? [laughs]

segments.speaker: william-chewey
segments.translation: Guess they found out how lazy I was [laughs].

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: When you was a teenager, did you ever kill pigs or kill chickens, or sometimes people go look for mushrooms, or fish, crawdads, hickory chicken. There’s no doubt that you experienced that stuff?

segments.speaker: william-chewey
segments.translation: Yeah, we didn't really fish that much. We usually used gigs, and like you said, crawdads. We would go – Ga-lon-nuski was her name – and her and her family, there was a Spavanalge Creek. We would go early in the mornings, but me and John, were just kids, but I remember they would cut them up and the other lady was my mother. They had some pans, and a pot of beans, and potatoes, and we would eat there. It was really good, and nowadays people don't do that, or they will have BBQ. Nobody really don't build a fire and cook anymore, or they won't dig potatoes either. And we would kill 'bout two or three pigs around Thanksgiving and we were scalding and scraping them. That's where I learn from, because me and John would have to get up early in the morning and we would have to go pull some water. Back then they put it in a barrel. They didn't pour water on them. They just put them in a barrel. It was nice back in the day, that you had all the tools to do it. He would do the water, like this and tell us the water wasn't hot enough yet. Then, when it got hot enough, he would tell us that, “the water was hot enough now, put the pig in there.” Then when they pulled them out, they would let the pigs cool down and then they would have to use a knife. They were pretty smart about doin' stuff like that.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: They used to use cast iron kettle. They would boil water in them. Anybody had a cast iron kettle back then, but nowadays you probably couldn't see one around hardly anymore.

segments.speaker: william-chewey
segments.translation: Yeah, I have three of them and one of them is pretty big. Someone that live right by the house gave it to me but I've never used it. Now whenever we have a reunion, even if the pigs are a little smaller, me and John used to cook the pig meat. I have a pot that I use for it.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: That reunion you're talkin' about, do you guys still do that?

segments.speaker: william-chewey
segments.translation: No, not that much. There is not that many of us anymore. Sometimes we would go to the creek, but when the pandemic hit, that's about the time we quit doing that. It went on 'bout three years, but then it got to where it was hard to get everybody together. Whenever that happened, there are only a few of us now. If they all agree to it, we would all go to the creek or somewhere.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: Man, it messed up a lot of people up, didn't it?

segments.speaker: william-chewey
segments.translation: Yeah, it sure did.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, that gave us a lot of problems, and messed everything up.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Let's say your wife, does she cook poke salad or wild onion? Does she cook that stuff?

segments.speaker: william-chewey
segments.translation: Yeah, that's pretty much all she knows – where to go pick wild onion – but she will never tell me where she goes. And then also we look for wild mushrooms, and then if I can beat her to it, hen of the woods. I know where they are at and I go pick them. She usually puts it in the freezer, and we would eat it around Christmas time, whenever we gather for Thanksgiving or Christmas.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Poke salad, too?

segments.speaker: william-chewey
segments.translation: No not poke salad, I don't know why but she don't like cooking poke salad. I guess because when you cook it, it don't make very much. [laughs] I went picked a lot one time and then she gave it all to her uncle, then I thought to myself, “I won't pick any more poke salad.” [laughs]

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: [laughs] So, you worked for no reason? [laughs]

segments.speaker: william-chewey
segments.translation: Yeah, for no reason.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: I bet you thought, “I can eat some,” too. [laughs]

segments.speaker: william-chewey
segments.translation: But wild onion was her main thing, because right by where we live there is a holler and that's where we find some.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: How 'bout... long time ago, old Cherokees that knew medicine, like the roots. They would say, “This right here will help you,” they would say. I wish I would've listened to more of that stuff.

segments.speaker: william-chewey
segments.translation: I wasn't so smart back then. If I was, I would've learned all that stuff, because my mom used to know all that stuff, like you said. I think I still know a little bit like when they cough or if they catch a cold, stuff like that.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: What kind is that?

segments.speaker: william-chewey
segments.translation: That stuff they call wild cherry. Like when you take a little bit of the layer underneath, it's red, and then you boil it for a little bit. After it boils for a little bit, then you drink it. It's really strong. I mix mine with honey. Like I told you, them little kids, they use it, too. When they get sick, they will call me on the phone and tell me to get some for us. “That's what we want.” It's really good medicine for coughing and just having a cold, and also… dang can't remember what they call it. I think in English, they call it spice wood. My father really used to like that kind of medicine. He drank it all the time. Even if he ain't sick he still drinks it. But you do the same thing to it, you boil it.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Some people knew how to do that kind of stuff.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: It's given to a Cherokee to make medicine like that.

segments.speaker: william-chewey
segments.translation: Right, yeah, you're right. It is given to us, and even us speaking Cherokee, it's given to us. A long time ago there is an old man. He that was learning, was talkin' to me, and he said, “Make sure you listen if an elder man or woman is speaking. That's where you will learn the most.” That's what he was telling me, because it's given to us, and nowadays the fewer that speak it 'bout three of them, the Cherokee running out. If we go to the woods, there is wild onion, hen of the woods, crawdads, it's all dying out. You ain't supposed to sell that stuff – a lot of people are selling it. Because it’s given to us Cherokee or Indians. That's why you ain't supposed to sell it. They say it's been given to us by God, and I never really thought about it like that, and then I thought. “That’s true what they are saying.”

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Nowadays, like you said crawdads. People are selling them.

segments.speaker: william-chewey
segments.translation: Yeah, they do sell them. I told someone I wouldn't pay for them. I told, “You can just give them to me. I'll take them, but I won't buy them,” I told them.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: Or like wissy. They sell them for 50 dollars.

segments.speaker: william-chewey
segments.translation: Yeah, real quick, they would sell ‘em for 50 dollars.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: Yeah, if I find one, I ain't going to sell it – I'm going to eat it. [laughs]

segments.speaker: william-chewey
segments.translation: Yeah, me either. I wouldn't sell it, because nowadays it ain't just us Cherokees or Indians that look for it. It’s white people, too. They heard 'bout it, so now they look for stuff like that. Mostly mushrooms, the ones that grow in the beginning of summer. It's hard to beat people to them anymore.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, someone said one time that the things that are given to us, you ain't supposed to sell it. But now, if you wanted to trade something for it, you can trade, as long as if it something that lives in the woods or wild, because that's just means you're just helping each other out. Now, if you're selling it, you ain't supposed to do that.

segments.speaker: william-chewey
segments.translation: But myself I really never find enough for me to sell, because I never look for it that much, because if I worked that hard to go get it then I ain't gonna sell it because I'm gonna eat it. [laughs] But now I will give it to someone if I find a lot of things. I'll just give it to someone, or I tell them to come to the house. “This is what we are gonna eat,” I tell them, “And we will have good meal.”

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Long time ago, when I was working for the county, guy by the name of John Gord, we used to work together. You know a guy by the name Cleve Smith? He was our boss.

segments.speaker: william-chewey
segments.translation: Yeah I know him.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: He asked him, “Well, what do you want us to do today?” he asked. “Well, just go out there and cut tree limbs,” he said. Well, we took off. We went towards Zena. We were driving really slow, and then John said, "Do you see them? I said”, “What?” He said, “You don't see them?” He stopped. “You don't see them?” “What does he see?” I thought. We got closer. There were wissy 'bout four of them. When we got back, Cleve was walkin' our way. He asked us, “Where you guys been?” We told them we went to north a little bit. He got close, he asked us, “What you got in back Mr Gord?” “Ohh, wissy,” he told him. “Goood eating,” John said. He asked, “How you fix it?” He told, “Cut it up, clean it real good and cook it,” he told him. He said, “Mind if I take one?” he said. Man, he picked the biggest one. The next day, we asked, “Well where do you want us to go Cleve?” He told us, “Go hunt some more wissy. [laughs] We went the whole week looking for wissy! [laughs]

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: And y'all were working for the county?

segments.speaker: william-chewey
segments.translation: And they were paying y'all for it. [laughs]

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Whenever you see a sign that says Cherokee, what is the first thing you think about? Do you think about how us Cherokees are living these days or them kind of thoughts don't come to you?

segments.speaker: william-chewey
segments.translation: I don't know about anything like that. I guess if I'm in that very moment I do, but I guess I would think about it more if I was towards Vinita. There ain't very many Cherokees there, but when you get to the clinic there is a big sign that says Cherokee. And when you go somewhere around here, all the roads and stuff, it's all in Cherokee. You would think, “Is there really a Cherokee working when I pass by?” That's what I think about, all that. I don't know if it's any good or not but that's what I think about.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: And another thing, too, if I see a sign in Cherokee, I think about what's happening to us Cherokees. And like we was talkin' about earlier, if someone trips and falls we just laugh about it. [laughs]

segments.speaker: william-chewey
segments.translation: And really, we grew up in Cherokee like you're talkin' about – when someone falls we won't ask them if they are OK. We will laugh at them first. Some of them, they won't understand like how it was or how we grew up back then and now. And also, like you're saying, the Cherokee, they prolly think about it but... And where we stand, that there is Cherokee writing everywhere. I wonder if they ever think about it, because it was hard for a Cherokee Indian growing up from the old times to now. Where we are now, they are now realizing that we are losing our language.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Long time ago, I remember an elder sayin' that you're always gonna have two strikes against you while you're growing up, sometimes you're gonna struggle in life while you're growing up being a Cherokee. You're gonna have to look for job sometimes because they will shut you down being a Cherokee. And then they will give the job to person that’s not Cherokee. Even if you're a good worker, they will still give it to someone else, but don't give up.

segments.speaker: william-chewey
segments.translation: My girls when they got to the age where they understood, I told them, “There ain't nobody better than y'all. We are all the same.” My belief is not like that, because when we started our first day there, 'bout two or three of us was sittin' last in the back row. We were all talkin' in Cherokee and then someone would tell on us, and the teacher would walk by and beat our hand with a ruler. That's when I got mad at Jay. I told them whenever I get a chance I was gonna quit or move schools. But then my parents find out, but they always seen it that you had to go to school and get education or you will never amount to anything if you don't go to school or get an education, that's what they were thinking. So that's when they pushed me this way. Well, everybody, John and Bebe, and also Wig, they all went to Oaks School. And me they put me little too far away. [laughs]. John would run away and come back to the house. [laughs] And myself, I couldn't get away because I was too far away.

segments.speaker: michael-cooksey
segments.translation: Were you speaking both languages, Cherokee and English, when you started school? Or was you only speaking Cherokee?

segments.speaker: william-chewey
segments.translation: All I was speaking was Cherokee. Do you remember Bud Arch? He was a bus driver. We became enemies real quick. Whenever something happened, usually they would put the person that did something wrong in the front seat. I was sitting on the steps – it didn't matter how cold it was, I was always sitting where the steps were. I was thinkin' I was doing good because I wasn't against anyone. I guess that’s what Bud Arch thought.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: I don't know why, but I remember Bud Arch. He really never liked Indians.

segments.speaker: william-chewey
segments.translation: Yeah, something happened between him and the girls. And my father told, “If you get out of that bus…” But Bud Arch never got out of that bus. [laughs] My father was little, but they say he was mean.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, he was mean.

segments.speaker: william-chewey
segments.translation: Yeah, me and John, we were bigger but we were scared of him. [laughs]

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: I remember when they were teenagers John and Goul, when they lived by the creek by Stick Springs, there used to be white person living there that had a lot of kids.

segments.speaker: william-chewey
segments.translation: Holker was their name.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: There were cows coming through there and John picked up a rock and threw it as hard as he could and he hit one of them baby calf and the boy hollered, “Hey!” He said, “I'm telling my dad on you!” he said. “Go ahead,” he said. “I'm going to kill another one!” [laughs] Later on, there came his dad walkin' up and he was mad, and he said, “John, you been hittin' my cows with rocks?” Huh, he was standing there grippin' at John and his dad heard him and he came walking outside and he said, “Watcha doing to my boy?” And he said, “He was hitting my cows with rocks!” he told him. He said, “He better not be doing that.” John’s dad asked him, “John, were you really doing that?” “Uh-uh.” [laughs] “There was a gate. He went through there and threw that rock hit it and it fell over” [laughs] It got up and started walkin' backwards and he asked his son, “Are you sure, John? You didn't do that?” [laughs]

segments.speaker: william-chewey
segments.translation: Yeah, my father, he was not scared of anyone.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: We would just be laughing and leave. [laughs]

segments.speaker: william-chewey
segments.translation: Yeah, I think I remember. I was in the yard whenever he and Holker got into it. Well, they really didn't get into it. He just hit him one time and that was it. [laughs]

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: We were walkin' by the church and we were all laughing. [laughs]

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Egleick was his name. I guess you was with us sometime at Piney Church in the afternoon. My sister was the driver.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: At some point and time, did you struggle learning or speaking English? Like you said earlier, you said the teachers didn't like us speaking Cherokee.

segments.speaker: william-chewey
segments.translation: I find out, too, that people from Jay- like the kids from Jay that lived in town - were different from country people like we was, because they were the ones that learned to speak English real quick. I remember before I went to school, there were some people from Jay by the name of Woods. They had a bait shop, and he used to trap minnows by the creek by our house and I watched him. Whenever he would turn around, I would hide somewhere. I didn't want him to see me. I didn't speak English at that time. I guess he saw me, but I didn't know.

segments.speaker: william-chewey
segments.translation: One time he left a little piece of bread – he was using a lot of bread to trap the minnows. So I found a piece of lot bread, and I ate it and I've never ate storebought bread. All we knew was biscuits back then. So, I brought it to the house. “So where did you get this at?” they asked. So I told them, and they said, “Well eat it up. It yours – you found it,” they said. [laughs] But that was the first time ever ate that. If I wasn't following him around, I wouldn't have ate it. [laughs]

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Whenever I used to work at the clinic, them Dry boys, Eugene, Homer, they were laughing and they were talking loud. They would be talking in Cherokee. [laughs] We were talkin' one time in the hall and we were laughing and talking in Cherokee. Then later on, they called me in the office and they told me they had a complaint on me. I told them, “You do? What for?” They told me, “For talking too loud out there, laughing, and they think you guys are talking about the workers in Cherokee.” “No, we ain't talkin' about them. We have better things to talk about," I told them. [laughs] I was scolded not to, so later on we had a meeting. I told them, “These Cherokees that just walked in, ain't we supposed to be helping them out?” I thought, “That's what we were here for, to minister to our people,” I said. They didn't say anything. It went on for 'bout two weeks, nobody talked to me, the people that worked there.

segments.speaker: william-chewey
segments.translation: That's what I used to think. Whenever Jane was working, I used to help them a little bit, the Cherokees that didn't understand English. There were a lot of them that came in, because they didn't know what kind of medicine that they were giving them. I told someone that was going to church, “That's what y'all are supposed to do there. Supposed to be a Cherokee speaker working in all the clinics, because some of y'all don't know, or none of y'all church goers have never been in a clinic. Because if something happen to you, you all will go to a white person hospital.” That’s what I told them and they didn't like that! I still believe that to this day there are still people coming in that don't understand what kind of medicine they are getting that they are supposed to use, or how many times they are suppose to take it.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Sometimes whenever when I was working, if they gave a Cherokee medicine, they ask if they understand it, or know how to take your medicine. And they say, “Uh-huh,” and they won't understand how to…

segments.speaker: william-chewey
segments.translation: And we don't ever tell anyone if we don't understand. We just tell them “Uh-huh.” Every one of us are like that.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Then sometimes if they see me, they would look at me and ask me what it says. They say they don't understand it, and I tell them and they say “Oh hawa hawa.” I explain it to them in Cherokee. There been several times that's happened. Or sometimes the nurses will tell a Cherokee, “You need to go to the x-ray", and they just be standing there. “You need to go to the x-ray!" and they don't understand.

segments.speaker: william-chewey
segments.translation: No, they don't understand.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Later on, the nurse’s face will be red, when she seen me. I thought, “Man!” So I told her, “I'll take them back there,” so I thought to myself, “Boy!” Just thinking…

segments.speaker: william-chewey
segments.translation: Yeah, they will be the first ones if the nurses say anything or the workers, they get mad and they won't help them out. And they wouldn't talk to anybody, they won't say, “This person speaks Cherokee and I need some help.” They won't say that. They will just get mad.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, it's really like that.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Was it hard for you to learn how to speak English? Or did you struggle with some of it?

segments.speaker: william-chewey
segments.translation: No, I really don't remember, I guess I learned it pretty good. I guess I prolly wouldn't have learned it if I wasn't watching Lone Ranger when I was just a young boy. [laughs] Cisco Kid. [laughs]

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Were you talkin' like Tonto used to? [laughs]

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: I'm gonna ask you this question, what do you think yourself in your own mind, in several years from now – well if we live that long – like in 20 years from now, like it says here, do you think that the Cherokee language will still carry on?

segments.speaker: william-chewey
segments.translation: I believe it will carry on, because I think it is very important what we are doing now. One time I used to go to this old man. He used to live in Briggs. He is not alive now. They used to eat almost all the time. It was in the afternoon, we was sitting there. There were kids walkin' up and their mom lived just right there. They weren't really that close together. They used to live in Cherokee houses. They were walkin' up, and he said, “Them boys walkin' up, talk to them in Cherokee.” I told him, “OK.” So, I talked to them and they started talkin' and it was beautiful how them boys talked. It wasn't like they learn it off the computer. You could tell that they learned it way back when they grew up at. It's been a long time since I've heard little kids talking Cherokee, but really I was glad. We sat and talked really good for while, then they wanted to play. Like I was sayin', like if there is someone living in your house that speaks Cherokee, they are gonna learn a lot more. It's good what they are doing here but it’s better if a parent or their grandparents are at home, if they would talk all the time. Then they will learn it really good, what they are doin'. But it’s not like how we used to talk – that’s what we are gonna run out of, whenever we gone – myself, John Deewid, and Doode has already left. He was a speaker. There are a lot of them that are already gone that are speakers. “There’s a lot of them still alive, but they won't come out of their house.” That’s what John used to say, “There are so many Cherokee speakers in Christy,” he said, “But they won't ever write anything down. But then they are OK with not having anything. They are always laughing around. They are good with how they are living,” John said, “Well GO-ni-yo-i, they didn't have anything. They used to get one check and there was 'bout five of them living there, but if I ever went over there, there would be beans, and bread. You would be laughing the whole time. You was there but they never thought anything about it. They were all just laughing all the time having good time, as long as they were eating…”

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, they were all like that. They were always dragging Sequoia around. [laughs]

segments.speaker: william-chewey
segments.translation: He was talkin' about his boys one time, he was telling Johnson, “This is my son. He is a crazy Indian boy. [laughs] And here is my little boy, Sequoia. He barely survived.” I guess his mother passed away. He barely made it when he was a baby. Johnson said, “Yeah, I remember that lice almost killed him when he was a baby.” [laughs] That boy never felt sorry for nobody. [laughs] They said lice almost killed him. [laughs]

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: They were all funny.

segments.speaker: william-chewey
segments.translation: Johnson, like I said, he is really crazy. [laughs]

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: William, what do you think about what we are doing now? Like us talking in Cherokee. Do you think it's a good thing or what do you think?

segments.speaker: william-chewey
segments.translation: Yeah, it good. It’s good, what we are doing.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Us talkin' in Cherokee?

segments.speaker: william-chewey
segments.translation: Like I said, there really ain't nobody really close – well, there is Tony, I guess. If I visit him more often would be good – and Levi, but Levi, it's hard for them to talk Cherokee. That's how he is, he speaks really good, but in English, unless I talk to him in Cherokee then he will speak some Cherokee. But not really, because if he speaks first, he ain't gonna say, “Siyo.” He will say, “Hello.” [laughs] But like what we are doing, it's good. It's gonna be good. And if the kids will use what we are doing, then it would be really good.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, they might learn something.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Do you feel good about him working in the Cherokee Nation, tryin' to save our Cherokee language? Them elders that speak the Cherokee language are all leaving.

segments.speaker: william-chewey
segments.translation: Yeah, that complex and the theater, used to be they had a gathering 'bout four years ago and that was really good back then. All in Cherokee. We was all sittin' there – John, Robert, and Harry Ossoween. We were sitting there talking and we were laughing, and someone had a recording like this and recorded us talkin'. They would've seen that, us Cherokees, we get together and talk. This is what Cherokee Indians do. They really would've seen what we do, because I hadn't seen Harry in a long time, or everyone, because Robert didn't live around Jay back then either. If we are able to visit one another and nobody knows that they are being recorded and there are 'bout three or four of us – because really if you ain't using it, they could keep it for their self.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Woody Hair, do you remember him? He used to know a lot of things that happened a long time ago, but nobody was recording at that time.

segments.speaker: william-chewey
segments.translation: Yeah, that's what I'm saying, nobody was recording it, me and John. The Keetoowah, they interviewed us, too, me and my brother John. Yeah I think I was interviewing John.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, there is room for Keetoowahs to come here also.

segments.speaker: william-chewey
segments.translation: Yeah, that's good. That's good because we are all Cherokees and we all know the language and there ain't nothing different between us.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Because even if I meet with a Keetoowahs, we are always laughing around, telling stories in Cherokee rambling on, yeah.

segments.speaker: william-chewey
segments.translation: As long as we are eating, it would be a lot more laughing around. [laughs]

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Well, I'm glad you came.

segments.speaker: william-chewey
segments.translation: OK.
